left.label: 'Pull the lever: one death beats five'

explanation: Duty judges the act; utility judges the outcome. The frameworks can honestly disagree — which is why engineers must deliberate explicitly.

prompt: Scenario: the client leans on your estimates
instructions: You and two colleagues are mid-planning-poker. The client says the bid must come down or the contract walks. Decide.

pressure.text: Estimates say 40 days; the client demands 25 and hints the contract depends on it. The team looks at you. What do you do?

options.label: Trim the cards to 25 to keep the contract
options.note: Knowingly false estimates betray the team and future users.

options.label: Refuse to change the numbers, disclose the uncertainty and offer options
options.note: Honesty plus options: the ACS stakeholder-trust response.

options.label: Say nothing and let the loudest voice decide
options.note: Silence delegates your professional judgement to pressure.

falsified.text: The project 'commits' to 25 days, overruns to 43, and the client you tried to please terminates anyway. The team absorbs unpaid overtime.
falsified.title: Numbers bent
falsified.debrief: Falsified estimates help nobody: the overrun still arrives, now compounded by broken trust. Public and stakeholder interest outranks client pressure in the ACS Code.

silent.text: Estimates drift down under pressure. Nobody owns the numbers, so nobody defends them — the same overrun, with deniability instead of integrity.
silent.title: Diffusion
silent.debrief: Diffusion of responsibility is how groups misbehave. Professionalism means owning your estimate out loud, even when it costs.

honest.text: You hold the 40-day estimate, show the breakdown, and offer scope phasing: core in 25 days, remainder next. The client pushes back. Now what?

options.label: Offer the phased scope in writing with risks stated
Concede the 40 was 'pessimistic' to smooth things over
options.note: Same falsification, slower — and now documented as yours.

phased.text: The client accepts phased delivery. The team ships the core on time; trust — the currency the ACS Code protects — survives the negotiation.
phased.title: Held the line
phased.debrief: Duty (don't lie) plus utility (a shippable core) plus code (stakeholder trust first). Frameworks converge here: honesty with options.

explanation: Estimate pressure is the handout's own scenario (Example 4). The pattern generalises: disclose, document, offer options — never silently comply.
source: Lecture 5 slides (PDF p. 33); ethics handout Example 4

prompt: Under the ACS Code, public interest outranks loyalty to your employer or client.
confirm: Health, safety, environment and stakeholder trust come first — the Code says so explicitly.
explanation: True. Professionalism means the public's safety and trust constrain what any client or employer can ask of you.
